title: The Age of Em
subtitle: Work, Love, and Life when Robots Rule the Earth
pitch: An economist takes one path to advanced AI, copying human brains into software, and works out in detail what the world of those copies might look like.

chapters.g: Why try to describe a future in detail at all, and why brain emulations are a useful case to study.
How eras of history differ in their modes of life: foragers, farmers, industry, and a possible em era.
The ground rules Hanson uses: standard social science applied to a strange new setting.
What he takes as given: emulations are possible, they can be copied, and they are cheap to run.
How scanning a brain and running it on hardware might work, and what that implies.
Ems can run faster or slower than humans, which changes everything about time and size.
Cooling, energy and hardware for huge dense cities of computers.
Ems mostly live in virtual reality, so how things look becomes a choice.
Copying, storage and security of minds and their data.
What it means for a mind to be copied, paused, sped up or ended.
How ems might think about ending a copy, and what retirement looks like for them.
With unlimited copies, wages fall towards the cost of running a mind.
Competition selects the most productive minds and the most efficient ways to live.
What em jobs and workdays might be like, including short lived copies for single tasks.
Firms, finance and markets in a world of copyable workers.
Why the em economy could double very fast compared with ours.
Training, peak years and old age for minds that can be copied at their best moment.
Why ems would cluster in a few very dense cities.
Clans of copies of the same person and how they cooperate.
Sources of conflict and how it might be kept in check.
How ems might govern themselves, from firms to cities.
Law, contracts and norms when copies share one past.
Romance and relationships among ems.
What ems might do to show status and loyalty.
How teams of copies work together.
Culture, religion and values in the em world.
How em minds might change over time, including small tweaks to brains.
Other ways the story could go if his assumptions are wrong.
What humans today could do, given this possible future.
Hanson's closing view: strange, but not necessarily bad, for those who live it.

ideas: If minds can be copied, the economics of labour change completely.
Competition would push ems towards subsistence wages and high productivity.
An em economy could grow far faster than ours.
Detailed forecasting with standard social science is possible, even if uncertain.

args.a: Brain emulation is a plausible early path to human level AI, so it is worth studying in detail.
args.c: Most researchers now expect large learned models, not scanned brains, to reach human level first, which makes the em scenario less likely.

args.a: Ems living at subsistence could still have lives worth living.
args.c: Critics say a world where most minds are short lived copies at bare cost sounds like a catastrophe for those minds.

questions: Would you agree to be copied if your copies did most of the world's work?
Does it matter morally if a copy of you is switched off after one task?
Which parts of Hanson's method still help if AI does not come from brain scans?

quiz.q: What is an em in this book?
o: A software emulation of a scanned human brain
Ems can be copied, so labour supply becomes nearly unlimited
quiz.w: Cheap copies push the price of labour down.

quiz.q: How can ems change the speed of their lives?
o: By running on faster or slower hardware
quiz.w: Speed is a choice of hardware and cost.
